title: Neurologic Disorders
markdown:
CHAPTER 5

## Neurologic Disorders

## CONTENT OVERVIEW

- Vertigo
- Head trauma
- Concussion
- Bell's palsy
- Headaches
- Neuropathy
- Tremors
- Dementia/delirium

## NOTES

## VERTIGO

- Sensation of spinning, movement, or disequilibrium
- MANY etiologies: get a thorough history.

## Peripheral

- Within the vestibular system (inner ear)
- Examples: benign positional vertigo, otitis media, Menière's disease

## Is Vertigo Peripheral or Central?

- Full neurologic exam
- Dix-Hallpike maneuver: canalithiasis of the posterior semicircular canal (BPPV)
- HINTS: head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew (if abnormal-central etiology)

| Finding         | Peripheral                 | Central                        |
|-----------------|----------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Nystagmus       | Stops with visual fixation | Continues with visual fixation |
| Gait/balance    | Normal                     | Impaired                       |
| Hearing         | May be impaired            | Normal                         |
| Neurologic exam | Normal                     | Impaired                       |

## Peripheral Vertigo Features

Episode length and characteristic features can help in identifying the cause of vertigo.

|                       | Etiology                  | Duration               | History Findings                                               | Physical Exam                                                   |
|-----------------------|---------------------------|------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Peripheral etiologies | Benign positional vertigo | Seconds                | Triggered by position changes Associated with nausea/vomiting  | Positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver                                  |
|                       | Vestibular migraine       | Few minutes to hours   | History of migraine, visual aura, photophobia, severe headache | Abnormal balance during episodes                                |
|                       | Vestibular neuritis       | Days, single episode   | Preceding viral syndrome                                       | Horizontal nystagmus toward healthy ear, resolves with fixation |
|                       | Ménière's disease         | 20 minutes to 12 hours | Spontaneous episodes, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus       | Low- or mid-frequency hearing loss                              |

## Central

- Involves the brainstem or cerebellum
- Examples: stroke, multiple sclerosis, brain tumor, meningitis

## Central Vertigo Features

|                    | Etiology                  | Episode Duration          | History Findings                                                   | Physical Exam                                                                    |
|--------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Central etiologies | Transient ischemic attack | Usually <1 hour           | Vascular risk factors, older age Sudden onset, single or recurrent | Temporary neurologic deficits Multidirectional nystagmus                         |
|                    | Stroke                    | Days to weeks, persistent | Vascular risk factors Sudden onset                                 | Neurologic deficits, may have hemodynamic instability Multidirectional nystagmus |
|                    | Multiple sclerosis        | Hours to days             | Fatigue, sensory loss; may have relapsing, remitting symptoms      | Optic neuritis Intermittent neuropsychiatric changes                             |

## QUESTION #1

A patient who has vertigo is examined. Which assessment finding suggests a central etiology of vertigo?

1. Nystagmus stops when the gaze is fixed on a stable object.
2. Vertigo is associated with hearing impairment.
3. The patient's neurologic exam is normal.
4. The patient is unable to maintain balance while walking.

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #2

Ms. H presents with intermittent dizziness and nausea. A Dix-Hallpike maneuver is performed. Which of the following would be considered a positive Dix-Hallpike?

1. Dizziness resolves immediately upon performing the maneuver.
2. A doll eye (oculocephalic) reflex is observed.
3. Nystagmus of <60 seconds is observed.
4. The patient vomits on the NP's shoes.

What is the patient's likely diagnosis?

## Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo

Managed in primary care

- Repositioning maneuvers (Epley maneuver)
- First-generation antihistamines
- $ Best evidence: meclizine (Antivert) 25-100 mg
- $ Reserved for highly disruptive symptoms
- $ Watch for anticholinergic side effects!
- Symptom management with anti-nausea medications

<!-- image -->

TIP: Refer for everything except BPPV!

## NOTES

## QUESTION #3

A 65-year-old patient fell and struck their head 2 hours ago. The patient should be referred to the ER for CT of the head if:

1. the patient's current Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 15.
2. the patient vomited once after the injury.
3. there is a laceration on the forehead.
4. the patient is 65-years old.

## Head Trauma Imaging Criteria

## Neurologic deficits

- GCS <13 at initial assessment or <15 2 hours after injury
- Seizure associated with injury
- Vomiting two or more times
- Retrograde amnesia >30 minutes

New Orleans Criteria (NOC) Guidelines Canadian CT Head Injury/Trauma Rule (CCHR)

## Concussion

## Mild acute traumatic brain injury

<!-- image -->

- Expected course
- $ Progressive symptom improvement within 7-10 days
- $ Symptom resolution by 1 month
- $ May need accommodations for school or work
- Common symptoms
- $ Emotional lability or irritability
- $ Headaches
- $ Dizziness
- $ Abnormal balance
- $ Mental fogginess
- $ Concentration or memory deficits
- $ Sleep changes

TIP: Refer if signs of neurologic decompensation

## Suspected skull fracture

- Open, depressed, or basilar skull fracture
- Signs: hemotympanum, periorbital bruising, otorrhea, rhinorrhea

<!-- image -->

## Risk factors for intracranial bleeding

- Bleeding disorder or anticoagulant treatment
- High-velocity injury (e.g., motor vehicle accident, fall >3 feet)
- Age >60 (NOC)
- Age ≥65 (CCHR)

## QUESTION #4

A 12-year-old sustained a mild concussion today during cheerleading practice. The neurologic exam is normal. The patient is advised to return to full activity:

1. after 48 hours of physical and cognitive rest.
2. when the patient can tolerate a full day of school activities.
3. when the headache has resolved completely.
4. after a 6-day return-to-play protocol without recurrent symptoms.

## Graduated Return to Play

<!-- image -->

If symptoms recur, must go back to previous step for minimum of 24 hours. Do not advance until resolution of symptoms.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Bell's Palsy Clinical Presentation

- CN VII palsy
- Idiopathic, acute, and spontaneous facial paralysis
- Clinical diagnosis
- House-Brackmann scale
- $ Grades severity from I (normal) to VI (complete paralysis)

## Bell's Palsy: Management Medical management depends upon severity

<!-- image -->

Medical management depends upon severity (House-Brackmann [H-B] grade) (House-Brackmann [H-B] grade)

| Glucocorticoids Glucocorticoids                            | Antivirals Antivirals                         |
|------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| All H-B Grades All H-B Grades                              | H-B Grade IV or higher H-B Grade IV or higher |
| Initiate ≤72 hours onset Initiate ≤72 hours onset          | Evidence of herpes Evidence of herpes         |
| 60-80 mg daily ×7 days, then taper 60-80 mg daily ×7 days, | then                                          |

taper

## Peak symptoms

· 1-2 days

## Stable symptoms

- 3 weeks

## Improved symptoms

- 2-3 months

## Recovery

· 3-6 months

TIP: Prevent complications: corneal abrasion and psychological distress

## Headaches

## DEFINED AS EITHER PRIMARY OR SECONDARY

- Primary headaches
- $ Caused by overactivity of pain-sensing structures in the brain
- $ Types: migraine, tension, cluster
- Secondary headaches
- $ Underlying pathology causes headache
- $ Often have "red flag" symptoms
- $ Examples: sinusitis, medication overuse, hypertension, stroke

## HEADACHES

## QUESTION #6

Which clinical feature of headache suggests the need for intracranial imaging?

1. Explosive eye pain resolving in 1 hour
2. Severe headache in patient taking dabigatran
3. Associated with nausea and vomiting
4. Visual distortion occurred pre-headache

## Headache Red Flags

| SNOOP-10 Headache Red Flags Suggest a secondary or emergent cause of headache   | SNOOP-10 Headache Red Flags Suggest a secondary or emergent cause of headache   | SNOOP-10 Headache Red Flags Suggest a secondary or emergent cause of headache   |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| S                                                                               | Systemic symptoms Secondary risk factors                                        | Systemic symptoms Secondary risk factors                                        |
| N                                                                               | Neurologic symptoms (altered mental status)                                     | Neurologic symptoms (altered mental status)                                     |
| O                                                                               | Onset is abrupt (thunderclap)                                                   | Onset is abrupt (thunderclap)                                                   |
| O                                                                               | Older (new or progressive in adults >50 years of age)                           | Older (new or progressive in adults >50 years of age)                           |
| P                                                                               | Pattern change Papilledema Positional Precipitated by Valsalva Progressive      | Pregnancy Posttraumatic Painful eye Pathology of immune system Painkiller use   |
| 10                                                                              | 10/10 in severity                                                               | 10/10 in severity                                                               |

## Papilledema

Swelling of the optic disc due to increased intracranial pressure

TIP: Papilledema is almost always bilateral

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Etiologies of Secondary Headaches

| Etiology                                                    | Key History/Characteristics                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Cerebrovascular accident (CVA) or transient ischemic attack | · History of cardiovascular disease · Sudden onset of focal neurologic change; hemodynamic instability; abnormal neuro exam |
| Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri)  | · Transient vision changes · Papilledema                                                                                    |
| Subdural hematoma                                           | · History of trauma or blood thinner use · Insidious degeneration of neural function · May be unprovoked                    |
| Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis)                   | · Age >50 years · Temple pain, fever, fatigue, jaw claudication, vision changes · Elevated ESR/CRP                          |
| Trigeminal neuralgia                                        | · Acute, severe, stabbing pain of the unilateral face (5th CN branch distribution) · May have pain between attacks          |

## Migraine Without Aura

- Time: headache lasts 4-72 hours
- Characteristics: (at least two of the following)
- $ Unilateral, pulsating quality
- $ Moderate to severe intensity
- $ Aggravated by routine activity
- Associated symptoms: (at least one of the following)
- $ Nausea and/or vomiting, photophobia, OR phonophobia
- Number of attacks: five or more episodes
- $ Less than five attacks: "Probable Migraine Disorder"
- No other reason for the headache occurrence

International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD3)

## Migraine With Aura

- 25% of patients with migraine have an aura
- ICHD-3 Diagnostic Criteria
- $ Meets criteria for migraine headaches
- $ At least two attacks of migraine with aura
- Aura features
- $ Fully reversible visual, sensory, motor, brainstem, retinal, or speech changes
- $ Develop over 5-60 minutes preceding a headache

## Visual Aura

<!-- image -->

## Migraine Headaches

- Risk factors: female sex, age 30 to 39 years, genetic susceptibility
- Identify triggers

<!-- image -->

## Migraine: Acute Treatment

| Medication Class                                             | Examples of Medications                                                                    | Considerations                                                                                                            |
|--------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Simple analgesics                                            | Acetaminophen                                                                              | Best for mild to moderate headache                                                                                        |
| NSAIDs                                                       | Aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac                                                    | Consider contraindications and adverse effects; more efficacious when combined with triptans                              |
| Triptans                                                     | Sumatriptan, zolmitriptan, naratriptan, rizatriptan, almotriptan, eletriptan, frovatriptan | Contraindicated if basilar migraine, ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, Prinzmetal angina, uncontrolled hypertension |
| Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRPs) receptor antagonists | Zavegepant (Zavzpret); Ubrogepant (Ubrelvy); Rimegepant (Nurtec ODT)                       | Zavegepant is intranasal, others oral; Nurtec ODT is also prophylactic Expensive                                          |
| Serotonin agonist (5HT1-F)                                   | Lasmiditan (Reyvow)                                                                        | Not vasoconstrictive, may be safer than triptans for some patients May reduce nausea/vomiting Not first-line therapy      |

## QUESTION #7

Which of the following is true about prescribing triptans?

1. If one triptan doesn't work, switch to a different drug class.
2. Triptans should be limited to no more than 2 days per month.
3. Sumatriptan SQ is recommended for cluster headaches.
4. Triptans may never be given at the same time as NSAID.

<!-- image -->

NOTES

## NOTES

## QUESTION #8

Which of the following drug classes may cause medication overuse headaches?

1. Opioids
2. Triptans
3. Simple analgesics
4. All of the above

## Medication Overuse Headache

- ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria
- $ Presence of a preexisting headache disorder
- $ Headache occurs 15 or more days per month
- $ Regular overuse of acute medications for >3 months
- >10 days per month regular intake of ergotamine, triptans, opioids, or combination analgesics, or any combination
- >15 days per month of simple analgesics
- $ No diagnosis better explains the symptoms
- Management: withdrawal of overused medication; initiate prophylactic headache treatment

## Migraine Prophylaxis

- Indications
- $ Frequent or long-lasting migraine
- >4 attacks per month or >12 hours per migraine
- $ Significant disability or quality of life
- $ At risk for medication overuse headache
- $ Abortive treatments are ineffective, contraindicated, or result in adverse effects
- $ Menstrual migraine
- Initiation (3- to 6-month trial): Start at low dose, titrate to therapeutic benefit

## Migraine: Prophylactic Agents

| Class                      | Medications                       | Considerations                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|----------------------------|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Nonselective beta blockers | Timolol, propranolol, metoprolol* | · Angina, hypertension, anxiety, younger · SE: weight gain, fatigue, decreased BP or HR, activity intolerance, bronchospasm · Avoid in bradycardia! · Caution in asthma, diabetes mellitus, depression |
| Anticonvulsants            | Valproate                         | · SE: weight gain, somnolence, hair loss · Highly teratogenic                                                                                                                                          |
| Anticonvulsants            | Topiramate                        | · SE: weight loss, concentration, fatigue, anorexia, paresthesia · Avoid in pregnancy                                                                                                                  |
| Antidepressants            | Amitriptyline*                    | · Sedating, given in evening · SE: anticholinergic activity                                                                                                                                            |
| Antidepressants            | Venlafaxine*                      | · Panic disorder, GAD, SAD, MDD · SE: nausea, dizziness, insomnia                                                                                                                                      |

*Not FDA-approved for migraines

<!-- image -->

## Other Primary Headaches

|                     | Tension-Type                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Cluster                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|---------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Diagnostic criteria | 10 episodes with 2 of the following: · Bilateral · Pressing (nonpulsating) · Mild to moderate · Not aggravated by routine activity Both of the following: · <1episode of Photophobia or phonophobia · No nausea or vomiting | Five attacks Severe unilateral orbital/temporal pain Both or either · At least one (ipsilateral to HA) $ Conjunctival injection/lacrimation $ Nasal congestion $ Rhinorrhea $ Eyelid edema $ Forehead and facial sweating $ Miosis and/or ptosis · A sense of restlessness or agitation |
| Duration            | 30 minutes to 7 days                                                                                                                                                                                                        | 15-180 minutes Active time course; 4-8 times per day                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Treatment           | NSAIDs, aspirin Acetaminophen Acetaminophen-aspirin-caffeine No opioids or barbiturates                                                                                                                                     | Acute · 100% oxygen therapy · SQ or nasal sumatriptan Prevention · Verapamil*, glucocorticoids                                                                                                                                                                                          |

* = off-label

## QUESTION #9

A patient who has diabetes reports numbness and tingling of the toes bilaterally. Which statement is true of diabetic neuropathy?

1. Duration and severity of hyperglycemia are primary risk factors.
2. Symptoms typically begin with unilateral, distal paresthesia of a limb.
3. Diabetic neuropathy is reversible with adequate blood glucose control.
4. Foot inspections should be performed at least weekly to prevent amputations.

## Diabetic Neuropathy

- Distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN) = diabetic neuropathy
- 15-20% of patients with diabetic neuropathy have pain.
- Symptomatic neuropathy is not usually reversible.
- Prevention!

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Differential Diagnosis of Neuropathy

| Neuropathy                    | Examples                                                     |
|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Metabolic                     | · Diabetes (most common) · B12 deficiency · Hypothyroidism   |
| Toxic                         | · Alcohol                                                    |
| Diffuse motor without sensory | · Guillain-Barré syndrome · Myasthenia gravis                |
| Inflammatory/infectious       | · Sarcoidosis · Lupus · Lyme disease                         |
| Compressive                   | · Carpal tunnel syndrome · Tarsal tunnel syndrome · Sciatica |

## Pharmacologic Treatment of Diabetic Neuropathy

Most likely to be on certification exam

| Drug Class                                           | FDA-Approved Drugs    | Evidence-Based Off-Label Alternatives   |
|------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) | Duloxetine (Cymbalta) | Venlafaxine (Effexor)                   |
| Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs)                     | -                     | Amitriptyline Desipramine Nortriptyline |
| Gabapentinoids                                       | Pregabalin (Lyrica)   | Gabapentin (Neurontin)                  |

## QUESTION #10

A 62-year-old patient has a new-onset hand tremor. A diagnosis of essential tremor would be suspected if the tremor:

1. starts unilaterally and looks like pill-rolling.
2. is most apparent when the hand is supported.
3. is associated with generalized bradykinesia.
4. occurs at the end of goal-directed movement.

<!-- image -->

## Essential Tremor vs. Parkinson Disease

|                        | Essential Tremor                                                                         | Parkinson Disease                                              |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Onset                  | 20s-30s and 60s-70s                                                                      | Average age 60s                                                |
| Tremor characteristics | Bilateral action tremor Worse with anxiety or caffeine Improves with alcohol             | Resting tremor Begins unilaterally, then spreads bilaterally   |
| Associated findings    | Mild gait disorder may be present                                                        | Bradykinesia, rigidity, gait disturbance, postural instability |
| Diagnosis              | Clinical diagnosis once tremor present at least 3 years; rule out alternatives (thyroid) | Clinical diagnosis                                             |
| Symptom management     | Propranolol, primidone                                                                   | Levodopa                                                       |

## QUESTION #11

Based on the presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis causing each tremor?

| Tremor Characteristics                             | Most Likely Diagnosis   |
|----------------------------------------------------|-------------------------|
| Unilateral onset, affects the foot at rest         |                         |
| Symmetric, affecting the voice and head            |                         |
| Induced by valproic acid                           |                         |
| Managed with primidone or propranolol              |                         |
| Accompanied by bradykinesia and rigidity           |                         |
| Symptoms of anxiety, heat intolerance, and fatigue |                         |

<!-- image -->

## COGNITIVE IMPAIRMENT AND DEMENTIA

## Memory Deficits

|              | Age-Associated                                                                                                                                | Dementia                                                                                                                               |
|--------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Onset        | 30s, 40s, 50s, and up                                                                                                                         | After age 60                                                                                                                           |
| Progression  | Subtle decline                                                                                                                                | Insidious progressive decline                                                                                                          |
| QOL          | No disruption                                                                                                                                 | Significant disruption                                                                                                                 |
| Key features | Memory impairment · Slow processing speed · Conceptual reasoning (problem-solving) · Memory (delayed recall, remembering to take medications) | Memory impairment (Impaired ability to) · Recall recent events · Learn new things · Complete familiar tasks · Complete executive tasks |

## NOTES

## NOTES Dementia

Umbrella term for a group of disorders causing memory or cognitive impairments

| Diagnosis                          | Characteristics                                                                                                     |
|------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Alzheimer dementia                 | Insidious onset, progressive decline in multiple cognitive domains                                                  |
| Vascular or multi-infarct dementia | CVD; history of ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke; may cause rapid or slow decline                                     |
| Lewy body dementia                 | Early appearance of visual hallucinations, cognitive fluctuations, REM sleep disorder, with or without parkinsonism |
| Frontotemporal dementia            | Early alteration of personality, social and emotional behavior, primary progressive aphasia                         |

## Dementia Risk Factors

- Cardiometabolic diseases
- $ HTN, hyperlipidemia, obesity, diabetes
- Depression and isolation
- Cognitive and physical inactivity
- Smoking, alcohol
- Hearing loss
- Head injury
- Advancing age

## QUESTION #12

An older patient is brought to the clinic by a family member. The family member reports concerns of cognitive decline. Which of the following statements are true?

1. The patient should be examined without the family member's input.
2. The patient is always aware of their own cognitive impairment.
3. A thorough medication review should be completed.
4. Determine if the family member has medical power of attorney.

## Dementia: Approach to Workup

- Thorough history from patient and significant other, if possible
- Cognitive testing
- $ Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA)
- ≥94% sensitivity, ≤60% specificity
- Free, online, several languages
- $ MMSE: sensitive and reliable, but not free
- Diagnostics
- $ Laboratory testing to rule out look-alikes (CBC, B12, TSH)
- $ Identified biomarkers (CSF, serum, PET): Research is ongoing!
- $ Consider referral if diagnosis is unclear or atypical features!

<!-- image -->

## Always screen for depression!

Depression can worsen cognitive impairment.

## PHQ-2

## In the past 2 weeks, how often have you:

1. had little interest in doing things?
2. felt down, depressed, or hopeless?

## Presumptive Alzheimer Disease Diagnosis

1. Cognitive impairment in more than one domain
2. Significant, insidious decline from previous level of function
3. Pattern and severity of decline in cognitive function impairs ability to perform ADLs
4. Delirium and other mental disorders (depression, schizophrenia, etc.) have been excluded

| Domains of Cognition   | Domains of Cognition   | Domains of Cognition   | Domains of Cognition   | Domains of Cognition    | Domains of Cognition   |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|-------------------------|------------------------|
| Learning and Memory    | Language               | Executive Function     | Complex Attention      | Perceptual Motor Skills | Social Cognition       |

## Diagnosis: Probable Alzheimer Disease (AD)

Agreement between history and mental exam is highly suggestive of Alzheimer dementia.

## AD Pharmacologic Management

<!-- image -->

Patients may meet criteria for monoclonal antibodies lecanemab and doneanemab.

NOTES

## NOTES Neurocognitive Decline Management

Prioritize Safety!!!

- Safety alerts
- Locks on doors
- Locked medication cabinets

Minimize anxiety

- Distract and redirect
- Establish and maintain routine
- Calm and reassuring responses

## Neuropsychiatric Symptoms

- Assess for other causes
- Nonpharmacotherapy first-line
- Manage persistent symptoms
- $ Depression: SSRI, SNRI
- $ Delusions/hallucinations/agitation:
- Brexpiprazole (Rexulti)
- Antipsychotics (Olanzapine, quetiapine-off label)
- $ Sleep disorders: melatonin, suvorexant (Belsomra)

## QUESTION #13

A 70-year-old patient is brought to the clinic by a caregiver who has noticed progressive memory changes over the past 3 months. Which diagnosis is least likely to be causing this patient's symptoms?

1. B12 deficiency
2. Depression
3. Syphilis
4. Delirium

## Delirium

- Sudden, significant change in brain function
- Common etiologies
- $ Drug use: medication change, substance use
- $ Medical conditions: atrial fibrillation, electrolyte disturbance, dehydration, nutritional deficiency
- $ Infection: UTI, pneumonia
- $ Brain insults: head injury, intracranial infection
- $ Environmental disruption: hospitalization, sensory deprivation

questions.stem: Which of the following drug classes may cause medication overuse headaches?
options: Opioids
Triptans
Simple analgesics

All of the above Medication Overuse Headache - ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria - Presence of a preexisting headache disorder - Headache occurs 15 or more days per month - Regular overuse of acute medications for >3 months - >10 days per month regular intake of ergotamine, triptans, opioids, or combination analgesics, or any combination - >15 days per month of simple analgesics - No diagnosis better explains the symptoms - Management: withdrawal of overused medication; initiate prophylactic headache treatment Migraine Prophylaxis - Indications - Frequent or long-lasting migraine - >4 attacks per month or >12 hours per migraine - Significant disability or quality of life - At risk for medication overuse headache - Abortive treatments are ineffective, contraindicated, or result in adverse effects - Menstrual migraine - Initiation (3- to 6-month trial): Start at low dose, titrate to therapeutic benefit Migraine: Prophylactic Agents | Class | Medications | Considerations | Delirium Delirium - Sudden, significant change in brain function - Common etiologies - Drug use: medication change, substance use - Medical conditions: atrial fibrillation, electrolyte disturbance, dehydration, nutritional deficiency - Infection: UTI, pneumonia - Brain insults: head injury, intracranial infection - Environmental disruption: hospitalization, sensory deprivation Cranial Nerves EXAM CHECKLIST - Headaches - Concussion - Vertigo - Neuropathy - Tremors - Dementia vs. delirium - Bell's palsy - Cranial nerves - Know clinical presentation (subjective, objective findings) - Know how to diagnose - What is in differential diagnosis?
